time-value-of-money-calculator.quickAnswer: Payment = PV x i / (1 - (1 + i)^-n), where i is the periodic rate and n the number of payments. Example: a 500,000 loan at 8.5% annual for 5 years, paid monthly, needs a payment of 10,258.27 per month. Total paid is 615,496, of which 115,496 is interest. Longer terms shrink the payment but grow the total interest.
keyFacts: TVM (time value of money) says money today is worth more than the same money later.
The payment formula amortizes the loan so the balance hits exactly zero at the last payment.
Periodic rate = annual rate / payments per year; periods = years x payments per year.
Each payment splits into interest on the remaining balance plus principal repayment.
Early payments are mostly interest; late payments are mostly principal.
At 0% interest the payment is simply the amount divided by the number of payments.
howTo: Enter the loan amount or present value.
Enter the annual interest rate as a percentage.
Choose the payment frequency: monthly, quarterly, or yearly.
Read your periodic payment, total paid, and total interest.
time-value-of-money-calculator.formula:
Payment = PV x i / (1 - (1 + i)^-n).
PV = present value (loan amount), i = periodic rate (annual rate / frequency), n = total payments (years x frequency).
Example: 500,000 at 8.5% monthly for 5 years: i = 0.007083, n = 60; payment = 500,000 x 0.007083 / (1 - 1.007083^-60) = 10,258.27.
benefits: Gives the exact amortizing payment, not a rough divide-by-months guess.
Handles monthly, quarterly, and yearly schedules in one tool.
Shows the true cost of the loan through the total-interest row.
Useful for loans, leases, and valuing any annuity.
limitations: Assumes a fixed rate and equal payments; variable-rate loans differ.
Ignores fees, insurance, and taxes that real lenders add to payments.
Assumes payments at the end of each period (ordinary annuity).
Estimates only: your lender's amortization schedule is the final word.

faqs.a: Time value of money: the idea that money available now is worth more than the same amount later, because it can earn interest. All loan math, including this payment formula, is built on that principle.

faqs.q: Why is total interest so high?
faqs.a: Because interest compounds on the unpaid balance. On a long loan you pay interest on interest for years before the principal shrinks meaningfully. Paying extra principal early cuts total interest dramatically.

faqs.q: How do I lower my payment?
faqs.a: Borrow less, get a lower rate, or stretch the term. Stretching the term lowers the payment but raises total interest, so compare the total-paid row, not just the payment.
Slightly. More frequent payments reduce the balance faster, which trims total interest a little. The bigger factor is always the rate and the term.

faqs.q: What if the interest rate is 0%?
faqs.a: Then the payment is simply the amount divided by the number of payments. The calculator handles this automatically: with no interest there is no compounding to solve for.

faqs.q: Can I use this for a savings goal instead of a loan?
faqs.a: Yes. The same math values an annuity: enter your target as the present value and the expected return as the rate, and the payment tells you what to save each period to reach it, ignoring that savings usually compound forward rather than amortize backward.
